howto.name: How to prepare for the proposed outbound investment rule

steps.name: Check whether you are a U.S. person under the rule
steps.text: The proposal reaches U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents, entities organized under U.S. law and their foreign branches, any person in the United States, and the foreign entities a U.S. person controls.

steps.name: Screen investments for a country of concern link
steps.text: Look for covered foreign persons tied to China (with Hong Kong and Macau), Cuba, Iran, North Korea or Russia, including entities that draw more than 50 percent of a key financial metric from such persons.

steps.name: Decide whether the target develops an SI system
steps.text: Under the proposal any development of an SI system is a prohibited technology, with no compute threshold. Building an agent harness on a third party model counts. Using an off the shelf third party system strictly for internal, non commercial purposes does not count on that basis alone.

steps.name: Comment by December 7, 2026
steps.text: File comments through regulations.gov under Docket No. TREAS-DO-2026-0595. Treasury asks in particular for comment on defining prohibited technology to include the development of any SI system.

steps.name: Keep applying Part 850 until a final rule takes effect
steps.text: The current regulations at 31 CFR Part 850 continue to apply to activity on or after January 2, 2025 and before the effective date of the final rule.

short: Treasury's proposed rule under the COINS Act would bar U.S. persons from covered investments in companies from countries of concern that develop any super intelligence (SI) system, the term the rule uses in place of AI system. Comments close December 7, 2026. The rule is proposed, not final.
title: Treasury Outbound Investment Rule (COINS Act)
subtitle: Proposed rule, 31 CFR Part 851: comments close December 7, 2026
body_html:
On this page

  • Where it stands
  • What it is
  • AI and super intelligence systems
  • Who is covered
  • Countries of concern
  • The six technology areas
  • Part 850 and the proposal compared
  • Exceptions
  • Penalties
  • The timeline
  • Sources

The U.S. Department of the Treasury has proposed new outbound investment regulations, 31 CFR Part 851, to implement the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act of 2025 (the COINS Act). For AI, the central change is this: a U.S. person would be prohibited from making a covered investment in a company from a country of concern that develops any super intelligence (SI) system. The current rules prohibit some AI investments and require notice of others, depending on computing power and end use. The proposal drops those lines. It is not a ban on all AI deals: it applies to covered transactions with covered foreign persons, and it has exceptions.

Where it stands

This is a proposed rule. It is not in force, and anything in it can change before a final rule. Treasury issued the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on October 22, 2026, and the Federal Register published it on October 26, 2026 at 91 FR 67396 (document 2026-21786, Docket No. TREAS-DO-2026-0595, RIN 1505-AC94). Written comments must be received by December 7, 2026, through regulations.gov. Until a final rule takes effect, the existing Outbound Investment Security Program regulations at 31 CFR Part 850 continue to apply. The effective date will be set in the final rule.

What it is

Congress enacted the COINS Act on December 18, 2025 as part of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026. It is codified at Title VIII of the Defense Production Act. Subtitle C directs the Secretary of the Treasury to do two things: require U.S. persons to notify Treasury of certain transactions involving covered foreign persons engaged in notifiable technologies, and prohibit U.S. persons from certain other transactions involving covered foreign persons engaged in prohibited technologies. The Act builds on the Outbound Investment Security Program that Treasury has run under Part 850 since January 2, 2025.

The program does not screen deals. The U.S. person making an investment has to work out whether it is prohibited, permitted with notification, or outside the rule. Treasury says it does not intend to publish a list of covered foreign persons.

AI and super intelligence systems

The proposal uses the term super intelligence (SI) system where Part 850 says AI system. Treasury explains that Executive Order 14434 of September 29, 2026 requires agencies to use Super Intelligence and SI in place of Artificial Intelligence and AI in certain documents. The thing regulated is the same kind of system: under proposed section 851.232, an SI system is a machine based system that can, for human defined objectives, generate content or make predictions, recommendations or decisions influencing real or virtual environments. The words generate content are there to capture generative models that produce text, audio, images, multimedia or code.

The definition also covers any data system, software, hardware, application, tool or utility that operates in whole or in part using such a system. The rule names two examples: an SI agent harness, and an embodied or physical SI system such as an industrial robot, a humanoid robot, an autonomous vehicle or an unmanned system.

Under proposed section 851.226(h), the development of any SI system is a prohibited technology. There is no notification tier for SI systems and no computing power threshold. Treasury's stated reason is that models now gain capability by means other than training compute, so that, in its words, no single measure, benchmark, or threshold is currently sufficient to distinguish advanced models. Two clarifications narrow and widen the word develop:

  • Building on someone else's model can count. A company that takes a third party SI system and enhances or extends its capability is developing an SI system. The rule's example is an agentic harness layer on a third party model that runs action loops, manages memory and context, or uses intermediate reasoning and self correction.
  • Internal use of an off the shelf system does not count by itself. Using an off the shelf third party SI system strictly for internal, non commercial purposes, including customizing, configuring or fine tuning it for internal use and not for sale or licensing, is not development of an SI system solely on that basis.

Treasury asks specifically for comment on defining prohibited technology to include the development of any SI system, and on the definition of SI system.

Who is covered

U.S. persons. Any U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident, any entity organized under the laws of the United States or a jurisdiction within it, including its foreign branches, and any person in the United States. A U.S. person also has obligations for its controlled foreign entities, meaning entities organized outside the United States of which it is a parent.

Covered national security transactions. Acquiring an equity interest or a contingent equity interest; certain debt financing that converts to equity or gives the lender certain rights; entering a joint venture; converting a contingent equity interest; a greenfield investment or other corporate expansion; a U.S. person's direction of certain transactions by a foreign person; and certain investments as a limited partner in a non U.S. pooled fund. The Act carries the concept of knowingly directing a transaction into the definition, so under the proposal it reaches notifiable transactions as well as prohibited ones.

Covered foreign persons. Citizens or permanent residents of a country of concern who are not U.S. citizens or permanent residents; entities incorporated in, headquartered in or organized under the laws of a country of concern; the government of a country of concern and those acting for it; members of the Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party and of the political leadership of a country of concern; entities majority owned or controlled by any of those; and an entity that holds an interest in covered foreign persons where more than 50 percent of one of several key financial metrics is attributable to them.

Knowledge. The obligations apply when the U.S. person knows the relevant facts. Knowledge includes actual knowledge, awareness of a high probability, and what a reasonable and diligent inquiry would have found.

Countries of concern

The Act and the proposal name the People's Republic of China, including Hong Kong and Macau; Cuba; Iran; North Korea; Russia; and Venezuela under the regime of Nicolás Maduro. Part 850 covers China, Hong Kong and Macau only.

Venezuela is in the text but does not currently qualify. Treasury's FAQ says the Maduro regime no longer exists, the United States recognized Delcy Rodríguez as head of state on March 5, 2026, and Venezuela therefore does not meet the proposed definition of a country of concern. Treasury still tells investors to check, because the rule can apply to some investments outside a country of concern.

The six technology areas

The Act lists five technology areas and lets the Secretary add others. The proposal adds biotechnology. A covered transaction with a covered foreign person engaged in a prohibited technology is prohibited; one engaged in a notifiable technology must be notified to Treasury no later than 30 days after completion.

AreaProhibited under the proposalNotifiable under the proposal
Semiconductors and microelectronicsElectronic design automation software, fabrication and advanced packaging equipment, the design or fabrication of certain advanced integrated circuits, and advanced packaging, as today. Added: radiation hardened and photonic integrated circuits, further categories of advanced chips, and high bandwidth memory with a memory bandwidth density above 2 gigabytes per second per square millimeter, which Treasury says aligns the rule with export control classification 3A090.Any integrated circuit activity that is not prohibited.
Super intelligence (SI) systemsDevelopment of any SI system.None. The notification tier is removed.
Quantum information technologiesQuantum computers and their critical components, quantum sensing platforms, and quantum networks or communication systems, as today. Added: development of algorithms or applications for quantum computing.None listed.
High performance computing and supercomputingSupercomputers, as today, and the added categories of advanced chips.High bandwidth, low latency interconnects for high performance computing.
Hypersonic systemsHypersonic systems and propulsion, certain related and enabling technologies, certain materials built for hypersonic conditions, and test facilities. New.Sensors, control equipment and software for hypersonic systems, and further dual use materials. New.
BiotechnologyCertain bio derived compounds and materials, brain computer interfaces, biomanufacturing equipment and facilities, equipment for biological design and sequencing, bioinformatics tools, and hardware or software for automated scientific discovery or experimentation. New.None listed.

A notifiable activity becomes prohibited when the covered foreign person, or one of its affiliates or subsidiaries, is on a listed U.S. government list. The proposal keeps the lists Part 850 uses, among them the Commerce Department's Entity List and Military End User List and Treasury's sanctions lists, and adds two: the list of Chinese military companies under section 1260H of the fiscal year 2021 defense authorization act, and the list of biotechnology companies of concern under the BIOSECURE Act.

Part 850 and the proposal compared

Question31 CFR Part 850, in force since January 2, 2025Proposed 31 CFR Part 851
AuthorityExecutive Order 14105 and the International Emergency Economic Powers ActThe COINS Act, Title VIII of the Defense Production Act
Countries of concernChina, with Hong Kong and MacauChina with Hong Kong and Macau, Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Russia, and Venezuela under the Maduro regime, which Treasury says does not currently qualify
Technology areasSemiconductors and microelectronics, quantum information technologies, AI systemsThe same three, with AI systems renamed SI systems, plus high performance computing and supercomputing, hypersonic systems and biotechnology
AI systemsSorted into prohibited, notifiable or not covered by the quantity of computing power used in training and by designed and intended end usesDevelopment of any SI system is prohibited. No compute threshold and no notification tier
Directing a foreign person's transactionKnowingly directing applies to prohibited transactionsApplies to notifiable transactions as well
Small transactionsNo de minimis exceptionTransactions of no more than $50,000 in aggregate over the preceding 12 months are excepted from the notification requirement only. This is not an exception to the prohibitions
Guidance on a specific dealNo such processA person with a direct financial interest in an actual transaction may ask Treasury for non binding feedback on whether it would be prohibited
Listed entities that turn a notifiable deal into a prohibited oneEntity List, Military End User List, Military Intelligence End User definition, sanctions lists and othersThe same, plus the section 1260H list of Chinese military companies and the BIOSECURE Act list

The Part 850 column describes the current rule as the proposal's preamble and Treasury's fact sheet describe it. Part 850 would continue to apply to activity that took place on or after January 2, 2025 and before the final rule's effective date.

Exceptions

The proposal excepts, among others: investments in publicly traded securities; securities issued by an investment company such as an index fund, mutual fund or exchange traded fund; a limited partner's investment in a non U.S. pooled fund where committed capital is no more than $2 million or the investor has a binding contractual assurance; derivatives of those; a full buyout of all covered foreign person ownership of an entity outside a country of concern; certain intracompany transfers from a U.S. parent to a controlled foreign entity; binding, uncalled capital commitments made before the final rule's effective date; certain syndicated debt financings; equity received as employment compensation; and transactions completed before the Act was enacted on December 18, 2025.

It also excepts secondary and ancillary transactions: procurement of material inputs, bank lending, payment processing and clearing, underwriting services, including the temporary acquisition of an equity interest solely to facilitate underwriting, and credit rating services. Contractual arrangements are excepted unless they transfer technology or technical knowledge. Certain exceptions do not apply where the investment gives the U.S. person governance rights beyond standard minority shareholder protections.

A U.S. person may ask for a national interest exemption from a prohibition. Treasury may also determine that another country is addressing the same risks, and except certain transactions involving persons of that country.

Penalties

A violation would be subject to civil penalties up to the maximum set in the International Emergency Economic Powers Act. The Secretary of the Treasury may compel the divestment of a covered transaction in a prohibited technology. The proposal sets out a voluntary self disclosure process, which Treasury would take into account in deciding its response.

Not later than 450 days after enactmentThe Act's deadline for Treasury to issue or update the regulations. Counted from December 18, 2025, that is March 13, 2027. The date is this site's count; Treasury states the 450 days
